stops.teaser: A capitol with no dome, just a low cone where one should be.
stops.map: Ohio Statehouse, Capitol Square, Columbus, OH
stops.clue: Go to Capitol Square in the middle of downtown, at Broad and High Streets. Look for the big Greek-style building with tall columns and a low, cone-shaped roof over the middle.
stops.safety: Capitol Square is busy and sits between busy streets. Use crosswalks, stay on the sidewalks, and follow any posted signs about events or fenced areas.

story: The Ohio Statehouse is where Ohio's lawmakers meet in Columbus. It was built between 1839 and 1861, which makes it one of the oldest working statehouses in the United States. The cornerstone was laid on July 4, 1839, before the commission had even agreed on a final design.

The most striking choice was to leave off the rounded dome that earlier designers had suggested. Instead, a low conical roof sits on top of the cupola over the rotunda, right where many visitors expect a dome. Fire destroyed the old two-story capitol building in 1852, and the exact cause is still a mystery.
Inside, the rotunda floor is made of almost 5,000 individual pieces of marble, all cut and fitted by hand. President Abraham Lincoln visited the building on three different occasions.
stops.fact: The cause of the 1852 fire in the old capitol was never found.
stops.disputed: Many people assume every state capitol has a dome. Wikipedia says this one dropped the dome on purpose, for a low conical roof.

claims.t: The Ohio Statehouse was built between 1839 and 1861.
The Statehouse has a rounded dome on top.
claims.why: Wikipedia says it has a low conical roof where many viewers expect a dome.

stops.teaser: A grand station torn down in 1976, except for one big arch.
stops.map: Union Station Arch, McFerson Commons, Arena District, Columbus, OH
stops.clue: Go to McFerson Commons park in the Arena District, just north of downtown. Look for a tall stone arch standing by itself, with columns on each side.
stops.safety: Stay on the park paths, use crosswalks to reach the park, and do not climb on the arch.

story: The first station on this site, built in 1851, was the first union station in the world, meaning several railroads shared one building. A bigger replacement went up in 1873 to 1875.

In 1893 Daniel Burnham, one of the main architects of the 1893 World's Columbian Exposition, began planning a new station. It opened in 1897, and its arcade along High Street was finished in 1899. The station's arches were framed by fluted columns, carved angels and decorative eagle medallions.

Passenger service fell sharply from the 1950s to the 1970s. The arcade was torn down in 1976 for a new convention center, even though it had been added to the National Register of Historic Places two years earlier. Train service stopped on April 28, 1977, and the rest of the station was demolished in 1979. One arch was saved, and it now stands in McFerson Commons.
stops.fact: The first building here was the first union station in the world.
stops.disputed: Many people think a listed historic building can't be torn down. Wikipedia says this one was on the National Register in 1974 and the arcade was demolished in 1976 anyway.

claims.t: Daniel Burnham designed Columbus Union Station.
claims.why: Wikipedia: Union Station was designed by Daniel Burnham.

claims.t: The whole arcade still stands along High Street.
claims.why: It was demolished in 1976, and only one arch was saved.

stops.name: LeVeque Tower
stops.teaser: A 47-story skyscraper built five inches taller than the Washington Monument.
stops.map: LeVeque Tower, 50 W Broad Street, Columbus, OH
stops.clue: Go to West Broad Street near the Scioto River. Look for the tall cream-colored tower with a stepped top and decorated crown.
stops.safety: Broad Street is busy. Use crosswalks and look up from the sidewalk. The tower is now a hotel and offices, so stay out of private areas.

story: The LeVeque Tower has 47 stories and stands 555 feet 5 inches tall. It was Columbus's tallest building from 1927 to 1974, and it is still the second tallest. When it opened it was the fifth tallest building in the world.

It was built as the American Insurance Union Citadel, headquarters for a fraternal insurance group. C. Howard Crane designed it in the Art Deco style, covered in cream-colored terracotta and inspired by Byzantine architecture. It cost $8.7 million.

The insurance group went bankrupt in the Great Depression. The building was renamed the Lincoln-LeVeque Tower in 1946 and the LeVeque Tower in 1977. After a long renovation, it reopened in 2017 as a mix of hotel, apartments, condos, offices and a restaurant.
stops.fact: It was made exactly 5 inches taller than the Washington Monument on purpose.
stops.disputed: Many people think the tower has always carried the LeVeque name. Wikipedia says it opened as the American Insurance Union Citadel.

claims.t: It has always been called the LeVeque Tower.
claims.why: It opened as the American Insurance Union Citadel and was renamed twice.

stops.teaser: A movie palace saved from demolition and still the state's official theater.
stops.map: Ohio Theatre, Capitol Square, Columbus, OH
stops.clue: Go to Capitol Square, across from the Statehouse. Look for the tall cream-colored building with arched windows and a marquee.
stops.safety: The streets here are busy. Use crosswalks and view the building from the public sidewalk.

story: The Ohio Theatre stands on Capitol Square on the site of the old Columbus City Hall. Thomas W. Lamb, a famous theater architect, designed it, and he called it one of his most successful. Inside, it was built to feel like a luxurious fantasy world, with rooms decorated in different themes.

It opened on March 17, 1928 as Loew's Ohio, a Spanish Baroque movie palace seating more than 3,000. The first film was The Divine Woman, a silent movie. The theater had its own orchestra and a Robert Morton organ that is still in use today.

Movie attendance fell in the 1950s and 1960s, and the theater was nearly demolished. A group formed in 1969 to save it, and it was later completely restored. It was declared a National Historic Landmark in 1977, and it is known as the Official Theatre of the State of Ohio.
stops.fact: The theater's original organ still plays.
stops.disputed: Many people think a historic movie palace has always been a concert hall. Wikipedia says the Ohio opened as a movie palace and later became a performing arts center.

claims.t: The Ohio Theatre was built as a concert hall for live shows only.
claims.why: It opened as Loew's Ohio, a movie palace.
